title: Keeping It Simple: What to Do When the Plan You Had Stops Making Sense
author: Heather McGonigal and Barbara Schindler
summary: Heather McGonigal and Barbara Schindler write up their episode on leading when the plan no longer makes sense. Their central claim is that under pressure teams add solutions until everyone is overstretched, and subtraction is often the better answer. They suggest pausing together and asking whether a simpler approach exists. They note that reactive, self-protective energy is contagious, so leaders who pause and choose from a steady place become a stabilising force. Not every external pressure needs an immediate response, since clarity often comes weeks later. The piece closes with takeaways, an action list and reflection questions.
points: Under stress, teams keep adding solutions until nobody can say why they are doing everything.
Leaders should ask 'How might we simplify what we're doing?' in the next team meeting.
Reactive energy is contagious, so a leader's pause and intentional choice steadies the team.
Some urgent-feeling pressures become clearer after eight to twelve weeks and need no immediate reply.
Scaling back may reveal the team has more capacity than leaders trusted.
quotes: When times get hard, teams start throwing solutions at the problem. They’re doing this, they added that, they took on one more thing to reach the goal, and soon everyone is stretched to the max and nobody can say why they’re doing all of it.
Pausing together with clear heads and asking whether there’s a simpler approach can reveal a lot.
Knowing how to pause and make an intentional choice from a steady place becomes a superpower.
Some of what feels urgent will be easier to read 8 or 12 weeks from now, when you have more information and can respond from more solid ground.
Human nature leans toward adding more to fix a problem, and the better answer is often subtraction.
External pressures don’t always need an immediate response. More will be revealed with time.
